text: Dubai has grown from a small pearling and trading port on the Persian Gulf into a global city of skyscrapers, artificial islands, and luxury tourism. Its rapid transformation reflects wealth and ambition in a desert setting.

title: Reykjavik geothermal note
text: Reykjavik, Iceland's capital, is heated largely by geothermal energy drawn from the volcanic landscape. Clean and compact, it serves as a base for visitors seeking geysers, glaciers, and the northern lights.

title: Venice sinking city note
text: Venice, built on wooden piles across a lagoon in northern Italy, faces the ongoing challenge of flooding and gradual subsidence. Its unique network of canals and bridges has made it one of the world's most distinctive cities.

title: Amsterdam below sea level note
text: Amsterdam, the Dutch capital, lies below sea level and is protected by an elaborate system of dikes, canals, and pumps. Much of the Netherlands has been reclaimed from water, a hallmark of Dutch engineering.

title: Cape Town Table Mountain note
text: Cape Town, one of South Africa's capitals, sits dramatically beneath the flat-topped Table Mountain. Its setting between mountains and two oceans, near the Cape of Good Hope, makes it one of the world's most scenic cities.

title: Luanda, Angola
text: Luanda is the capital and main port of Angola, on the Atlantic coast of Southern Africa. A rapidly growing city fueled by oil wealth, it is the country's political, cultural, and economic center.

title: Maputo, Mozambique
text: Maputo is the capital of Mozambique, a port city on the Indian Ocean. Known for its wide avenues, Mediterranean-style buildings, and lively markets, it reflects a blend of Portuguese and African influences.

title: Lusaka, Zambia
text: Lusaka is the capital of Zambia, set on a plateau in the south-central part of the country. It serves as the nation's commercial and administrative hub and a crossroads of major routes.

title: Abuja, Nigeria
text: Abuja is the purpose-built capital of Nigeria, established in the 1980s in the country's center. Known for its planned layout, government buildings, and the towering Aso Rock, it replaced Lagos as the seat of government.

title: Yaounde, Cameroon
text: Yaounde is the capital of Cameroon, set among hills in the country's interior. It serves as the political center of a nation known for its diversity, while the port of Douala is the largest city.

title: Bamako, Mali
text: Bamako is the capital of Mali, set on the Niger River. A busy commercial center and one of the fastest-growing cities in Africa, it is known for its markets and music scene.

title: Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso
text: Ouagadougou is the capital of Burkina Faso in West Africa. The country's cultural and administrative heart, it hosts a renowned pan-African film festival and lies in the semi-arid Sahel.

title: Lome, Togo
text: Lome is the capital of Togo, a port city on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa. Known for its beaches, markets, and coastal setting, it serves as the country's commercial and administrative center.

title: Conakry, Guinea
text: Conakry is the capital and largest city of Guinea, set on a peninsula and island on the Atlantic coast of West Africa. It is the country's main port and economic center.

title: Freetown, Sierra Leone
text: Freetown is the capital of Sierra Leone, set on a large natural harbor on the Atlantic coast. Founded as a home for freed slaves, it is the country's political and economic center.

title: Monrovia, Liberia
text: Monrovia is the capital of Liberia, on the Atlantic coast of West Africa. Named after an American president, it reflects the country's founding by freed American slaves in the 19th century.

title: Gitega, Burundi
text: Gitega is the political capital of Burundi, a small landlocked country in East Africa, while Bujumbura on Lake Tanganyika remains the largest city and economic center. The country lies in the Great Lakes region.

title: Asmara, Eritrea
text: Asmara is the capital of Eritrea, set on a highland plateau. Known for its remarkable collection of early 20th-century Italian modernist architecture, its historic center is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Mogadishu, Somalia
text: Mogadishu is the capital of Somalia, an ancient port on the Indian Ocean. A historic center of trade along the East African coast, it has a long and layered history stretching back many centuries.

title: Juba, South Sudan
text: Juba is the capital of South Sudan, set on the White Nile. It became the capital of the world's newest widely recognized nation when the country gained independence in 2011.

title: Nouakchott, Mauritania
text: Nouakchott is the capital of Mauritania, a city on the Atlantic coast at the edge of the Sahara Desert. Once a small settlement, it grew rapidly into the country's largest city and administrative center.

title: Bandar Seri Begawan, Brunei
text: Bandar Seri Begawan is the capital of Brunei on the island of Borneo. Known for its grand mosques and a large water village of stilt houses on the river, it is the small, oil-rich sultanate's main city.

title: Dili, Timor-Leste
text: Dili is the capital of Timor-Leste, a port city on the northern coast of the island of Timor. It serves as the young nation's political and commercial center following independence in 2002.

title: Nuku'alofa, Tonga
text: Nuku'alofa is the capital of Tonga, a Polynesian kingdom in the South Pacific. Set on the main island, it is the seat of the last Polynesian monarchy and the country's commercial center.

title: Honiara, Solomon Islands
text: Honiara is the capital of the Solomon Islands, on the island of Guadalcanal in the South Pacific. The site of major World War II battles, it is now the country's administrative and commercial hub.

title: Port Vila, Vanuatu
text: Port Vila is the capital of Vanuatu, a port town on the island of Efate in the South Pacific. It is the commercial center of an archipelago known for volcanoes and diverse traditional cultures.

title: Majuro, Marshall Islands
text: Majuro is the capital of the Marshall Islands, a narrow coral atoll in the central Pacific. As the country's largest settlement, it stretches along a thin ribbon of low-lying land encircling a lagoon.

title: Roseau, Dominica
text: Roseau is the capital of Dominica, a small city on the mountainous, volcanic Caribbean island. Set between the sea and steep green hills, it serves as the main port of the Nature Isle.

title: Bridgetown, Barbados
text: Bridgetown is the capital of Barbados, a port city on the Caribbean island's southwest coast. Its historic garrison and old town, reflecting the island's colonial past, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Castries, Saint Lucia
text: Castries is the capital of Saint Lucia, a port city on the Caribbean island set around a natural harbor. It serves as the commercial center of an island famed for its twin volcanic Pitons.

title: Basseterre, Saint Kitts
text: Basseterre is the capital of Saint Kitts and Nevis, a port town on the Caribbean island of Saint Kitts. It is the commercial heart of the smallest sovereign state in the Americas.

title: Andorra la Vella
text: Andorra la Vella is the capital of Andorra, the highest capital city in Europe, set in the Pyrenees mountains. It is a center for skiing, duty-free shopping, and mountain tourism between France and Spain.

title: Vaduz, Liechtenstein
text: Vaduz is the capital of Liechtenstein, a small town in the Alps along the Rhine. Overlooked by a princely castle on a hillside, it serves as the seat of one of the world's smallest countries.

title: City of San Marino
text: The City of San Marino is the capital of the microstate of San Marino, perched atop Mount Titano. Its medieval towers and walls, offering sweeping views, crown one of the world's oldest republics surrounded by Italy.

title: Valletta, Malta
text: Valletta is the capital of Malta, a fortified city built by the Knights of Saint John in the 16th century. Rich in baroque architecture and history, the entire small city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: Seven Wonders of Ancient World
text: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World were remarkable constructions listed by ancient Greek writers. They included the Great Pyramid of Giza, the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, and the Lighthouse of Alexandria, of which only the pyramid survives.

title: New Seven Wonders
text: In a global poll of the 21st century, seven sites were named the New Seven Wonders of the World: the Great Wall of China, Petra, the Colosseum, Chichen Itza, Machu Picchu, the Taj Mahal, and Christ the Redeemer.

title: UNESCO World Heritage Sites
text: UNESCO World Heritage Sites are places recognized for outstanding cultural or natural value to humanity. They include monuments, cities, and landscapes around the world, protected for future generations by international agreement.

title: The Hanging Gardens
text: The Hanging Gardens of Babylon were a legendary terraced garden counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Said to have been built in ancient Mesopotamia, no trace has been confirmed, and their exact nature remains a mystery.

title: Lighthouse of Alexandria
text: The Lighthouse of Alexandria was a towering ancient lighthouse on the coast of Egypt, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. It guided ships into the busy harbor for centuries before being destroyed by earthquakes.

title: Colossus of Rhodes
text: The Colossus of Rhodes was a giant ancient statue of the sun god Helios that stood at the harbor of the Greek island of Rhodes. One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, it was toppled by an earthquake.

title: Temple of Artemis
text: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, in what is now Turkey, was a vast ancient Greek temple counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Renowned for its scale and beauty, only fragments remain today.

title: Statue of Zeus at Olympia
text: The Statue of Zeus at Olympia was a colossal seated figure of the Greek god crafted in gold and ivory. One of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, it stood in the temple at the site of the ancient Olympic Games.

title: Mausoleum at Halicarnassus
text: The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus was an elaborate ancient tomb built for a ruler in what is now Turkey. So famous for its grandeur, it gave the word mausoleum to later languages and was one of the ancient wonders.

title: Panama Canal engineering
text: The Panama Canal is regarded as one of the great engineering achievements of the modern age. Its locks raise and lower ships across the continental divide, allowing them to pass between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.

title: Channel Tunnel
text: The Channel Tunnel is an undersea rail tunnel connecting England and France beneath the English Channel. Opened in 1994, it allows trains to travel between the two countries in about half an hour under the seabed.

title: Three Gorges Dam
text: The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River in China is one of the largest hydroelectric dams in the world. It generates vast amounts of power and helps control flooding, though it required relocating many communities.

title: Golden Gate as a wonder
text: The Golden Gate Bridge is often listed among the wonders of the modern world for its graceful design and engineering. Spanning the strait at the entrance to San Francisco Bay, it stood as the world's longest suspension span for years.

title: Itaipu Dam
text: The Itaipu Dam on the Parana River between Brazil and Paraguay is one of the largest hydroelectric plants in the world by energy production. It supplies a significant share of both countries' electricity.

title: Traveling with children
text: Traveling with children requires extra planning, including entertainment, snacks, and rest breaks. Families often benefit from choosing child-friendly accommodation and pacing their itinerary to suit younger travelers' needs.

title: Solo travel considerations
text: Traveling alone offers freedom and flexibility but calls for extra attention to safety and planning. Solo travelers often share their itinerary with someone at home and stay aware of their surroundings in unfamiliar places.

title: Budgeting for a trip
text: Planning a travel budget involves estimating costs for transport, accommodation, food, and activities, plus a margin for the unexpected. Researching prices at the destination in advance helps travelers avoid overspending.

title: Overcoming language barriers
text: When travelers do not share a language with locals, translation apps, phrasebooks, gestures, and simple drawings can bridge the gap. Patience and a friendly manner go a long way toward being understood abroad.

title: Public holidays abroad
text: Public holidays vary by country and can affect travel, as shops, banks, and attractions may close and transport may be busier. Checking the local calendar helps travelers plan around festivals and national days.

title: Traveling responsibly
text: Responsible travel means respecting local communities, cultures, and environments. It includes supporting local businesses, minimizing waste, protecting wildlife, and being mindful of the impact that visitors can have on a place.

title: Understanding time differences
text: The difference in local time between two places depends on how many time zones apart they are. Travelers making calls or connections across zones should account for whether the destination is ahead of or behind their home time.

title: Reading a world map
text: A world map shows the continents, oceans, and countries of the Earth. Understanding features such as the equator, the poles, latitude and longitude lines, and a scale helps a reader locate places and judge distances.

title: Great circle routes
text: The shortest distance between two points on the globe follows a great circle, a path along the largest circle that can be drawn around a sphere. This is why long flights curve on flat maps rather than following straight lines.

title: Understanding coastlines and tides
text: Coastlines mark where land meets the sea, and they change with the tides, the regular rise and fall of ocean water caused by the pull of the moon and sun. Coastal travelers should be aware of tide times for safety.

title: Indo-European languages
text: The Indo-European family is the largest language family by number of speakers, including English, Spanish, Hindi, Russian, and many others. Its languages are spoken across Europe, much of the Americas, and parts of Asia.

title: Romance languages
text: The Romance languages descend from Latin and include Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Romanian. Spread by the Roman Empire and later colonization, they are spoken across Europe, the Americas, and Africa.

title: Sino-Tibetan languages
text: The Sino-Tibetan family includes the Chinese languages, such as Mandarin and Cantonese, as well as Tibetan and Burmese. Chinese, with its many varieties, has more native speakers than any other language.

title: Bantu languages
text: The Bantu languages are a large group of related languages spoken across much of Central, Eastern, and Southern Africa. They include Swahili, Zulu, and Shona, and are spoken by hundreds of millions of people.

title: Writing systems of the world
text: Languages are written in many different scripts. The Latin alphabet is the most widespread, while others include Cyrillic, Arabic, Chinese characters, Devanagari, and Greek. Some scripts read right to left rather than left to right.

title: The Latin alphabet
text: The Latin alphabet, developed from ancient Rome, is the most widely used writing system in the world. It forms the basis for English, Spanish, French, and countless other languages, often with added marks for particular sounds.

title: The Cyrillic alphabet
text: The Cyrillic alphabet is used to write Russian, Bulgarian, Serbian, and several other languages, mostly in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. Developed from Greek letters, it is named after the missionary Saint Cyril.

title: Tonal languages
text: In tonal languages, the pitch or tone with which a word is spoken can change its meaning. Mandarin Chinese, Vietnamese, Thai, and many African languages are tonal, so pronunciation of tones is essential to being understood.

title: Lingua franca
text: A lingua franca is a common language used to communicate between people who speak different native tongues. English serves as a global lingua franca today, while Swahili, Arabic, and French play similar roles regionally.

title: Endangered languages
text: Many of the world's thousands of languages are endangered, spoken by only small or aging communities. Efforts to document and revive them help preserve the cultural knowledge and diversity that each language carries.

title: Roman Catholicism
text: Roman Catholicism is the largest branch of Christianity, led by the Pope in Vatican City. It is practiced worldwide, with strong followings in Latin America, southern Europe, and parts of Africa and Asia, and centers on the Mass.

title: Eastern Orthodoxy
text: Eastern Orthodoxy is a major branch of Christianity prominent in Eastern Europe, Russia, Greece, and the Middle East. Known for its icons, elaborate liturgy, and ancient traditions, it separated from the Western Church centuries ago.

title: Protestant Christianity
text: Protestantism is a broad branch of Christianity that arose from the Reformation in 16th-century Europe. It includes many denominations, such as Lutheran, Baptist, and Methodist, and is widespread in northern Europe and the Americas.

title: Sunni and Shia Islam
text: Islam has two major branches, Sunni and Shia, which differ over early leadership after the Prophet Muhammad. Sunni Muslims form the large majority worldwide, while Shia communities are prominent in Iran, Iraq, and nearby regions.

title: The Five Pillars of Islam
text: The Five Pillars are the core practices of Islam: the declaration of faith, daily prayer, giving to charity, fasting during Ramadan, and pilgrimage to Mecca. They shape the religious life of Muslims around the world.

title: Pilgrimage traditions
text: Pilgrimage, a journey to a sacred place, is important in many religions. Muslims travel to Mecca for the Hajj, Christians to sites such as Rome or Jerusalem, Hindus to the Ganges, and pilgrims of many faiths to holy destinations.

title: Hindu deities and beliefs
text: Hinduism reveres many deities, including Vishnu, Shiva, and the goddess Devi, seen by many as aspects of a single reality. Core ideas include dharma, or duty, karma, and the cycle of rebirth known as samsara.

title: Buddhist traditions
text: Buddhism has several major traditions, including Theravada, prominent in Southeast Asia, and Mahayana, widespread in East Asia. All share the teachings of the Buddha and practices such as meditation and mindfulness.

title: Indigenous belief systems
text: Around the world, many Indigenous peoples maintain their own spiritual traditions, often closely tied to nature, ancestors, and the land. These varied belief systems predate and coexist with major world religions.

title: Secular and non-religious populations
text: A significant portion of the world's people identify as non-religious, agnostic, or atheist, or follow no formal religion. Levels of religious practice vary widely between countries and regions.

title: Plate tectonics
text: Plate tectonics is the theory that Earth's outer shell is divided into large plates that slowly move. Their interactions create mountains, cause earthquakes, and drive volcanic activity where plates collide, separate, or slide past one another.

title: Earthquakes
text: Earthquakes are sudden shakings of the ground caused by the movement of Earth's tectonic plates. They occur most often along plate boundaries, such as around the Pacific Ring of Fire, and can range from barely felt to highly destructive.

title: Volcanoes
text: Volcanoes are openings in Earth's surface through which molten rock, ash, and gases erupt. Found mainly along tectonic plate boundaries and hotspots, they build mountains and islands and can dramatically reshape the landscape.

title: Glaciers
text: Glaciers are large, slow-moving masses of ice formed from compacted snow over many years. They shape valleys and coastlines, store much of the world's fresh water, and are found in polar regions and high mountains.

title: Ocean currents
text: Ocean currents are large-scale flows of seawater driven by winds, temperature, and salinity differences. They redistribute heat around the planet, influencing climate, weather, and marine life across vast distances.

title: The water cycle
text: The water cycle describes how water moves through the environment, evaporating from oceans and lakes, forming clouds, falling as precipitation, and flowing back through rivers to the sea. It sustains freshwater supplies worldwide.

title: Monsoons
text: A monsoon is a seasonal shift in wind that brings heavy rains to regions such as South and Southeast Asia. The summer monsoon is vital for agriculture, delivering much of the year's rainfall in a few months.

title: Deltas and estuaries
text: A delta forms where a river deposits sediment as it meets a sea or lake, creating fertile, branching lowlands. Major deltas, such as those of the Nile, Ganges, and Mississippi, support dense populations and rich farmland.

title: Peninsulas
text: A peninsula is a piece of land almost entirely surrounded by water but connected to a larger landmass. Examples include the Iberian, Arabian, Korean, and Italian peninsulas, each shaping the geography of its region.

title: Isthmuses
text: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land connecting two larger landmasses, with water on either side. The Isthmus of Panama joins North and South America and is crossed by the Panama Canal linking two oceans.

title: Archipelagos
text: An archipelago is a group or chain of islands. Notable examples include Indonesia, the Philippines, the Caribbean, and the islands of Greece, and such island groups often share related cultures and ecosystems.

title: Plateaus
text: A plateau is an elevated area of relatively flat land. Examples include the Tibetan Plateau, the highest in the world, and the plateaus of central Africa and the American Southwest, which shape climate and rivers.

title: Basins and watersheds
text: A drainage basin, or watershed, is the area of land where all water drains toward a single river or lake. The Amazon and Congo basins are among the largest, collecting rainfall over vast regions of forest.

title: Sea level and elevation
text: Elevation measures how high a place is above sea level, the average level of the ocean's surface used as a reference. The Dead Sea shore is the lowest land point, while Everest is the highest, and much of the Netherlands lies below sea level.

title: Cardinal and intermediate directions
text: The four cardinal directions are north, south, east, and west, while the intermediate directions, northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest, lie between them. Together they help describe direction precisely on maps and in navigation.

title: Hemispheres of the Earth
text: The Earth can be divided into hemispheres: the Northern and Southern by the equator, and the Eastern and Western by lines of longitude. Most of the world's land and people lie in the Northern Hemisphere.

title: The poles
text: The North and South Poles are the points where Earth's axis of rotation meets its surface. The North Pole lies in the frozen Arctic Ocean, while the South Pole sits on the icy continent of Antarctica.

title: Deserts and rain shadows
text: Some deserts form in rain shadows, where mountains block moist air and leave the far side dry. As air rises over a range it releases rain, so the leeward side receives little moisture, creating arid conditions.

title: Coral reefs and atolls
text: Coral reefs are built by tiny marine animals in warm seas, and atolls are ring-shaped reefs enclosing a lagoon, often formed around sunken volcanoes. They support rich marine life and protect coastlines from waves.

title: The changing map of the world
text: The political map of the world changes over time as nations gain independence, merge, or redraw borders. Studying geography includes understanding that boundaries and country names have shifted throughout history.
